concept: MongoDB Query Shape Optimization: Sort, Pagination, Operators and Sharded Targeting
summary: The shape of a find or aggregate query decides whether the planner can use an index: index-backed sorts avoid the blocking SORT stage and its memory limit, keyset pagination replaces deep skip, $regex, $ne, $nin, $where and $expr constrain index bounds, $in and $or become point bounds or index unions, projection can make a query covered, count, distinct, $sample and cursor batchSize/maxTimeMS carry their own costs, and a sharded query is targeted only when the shard key is in the filter. Compiled from MongoDB manual and Atlas pages plus the run's verified claims.

A query shape is a set of specifications that group similar queries together. Specifications can include filters, sorts, projections, aggregation pipeline stages, a namespace, and others. Queries that have similar specifications have the same query shape.

For instance, the inequality operators $nin and $ne are not very selective since they often match a large portion of the index. As a result, in many cases, a $nin or $ne query with an index may perform no better than a $nin or $ne query that must scan all documents in a collection.

Further optimization can occur if the regular expression is a "prefix expression", which means that all potential matches start with the same string. This allows MongoDB to construct a "range" from that prefix and only match values from the index within the specified range.

A regular expression is a "prefix expression" if it starts with a caret (`^`) or a left anchor (`\A`), followed by a string of simple symbols. For example, the regex `/^abc.*/` is optimized to match only the values from the index that start with `abc`.

Sort and limit behave differently in the router. Unsorted results come from a round-robin over shard cursors. With limit(), mongos passes the limit to each shard and re-applies it to the merged result. With skip(), mongos cannot push the skip down: it passes limit+skip to the shards, then skips while assembling results. Deep skip on a sharded collection therefore costs more.

If MongoDB cannot obtain the sort order with an index scan, then MongoDB uses a top-k sort algorithm. This algorithm buffers the first `k` results (or last, depending on the sort order) seen so far by the underlying index or collection access. If the memory footprint of these `k` results exceeds 100 megabytes, MongoDB automatically writes temporary files to disk unless the query specifies [`cursor.allowDiskUse()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.allowdiskuse.md#mongodb-method-cursor.allowDiskUse) with a value of `false` (in which case, the query fails).

Since reading.timestamp is not included in an index, MongoDB must perform an in-memory sort operation to return results in the requested sort order. By specifying cursor.allowDiskUse(false), MongoDB cannot process the sort operation if it requires more than 100 megabytes of system memory. If the operation requires more than 100 megabytes of system memory, MongoDB would return an error.

A compound index supports a sort on all its keys or on a prefix, with sort keys in index order. Directions must match the index pattern or its exact inverse: {a:1,b:-1} supports {a:1,b:-1} and {a:-1,b:1}, but not {a:1,b:1} or {a:-1,b:-1}.

An index can serve a sort on a non-prefix subset of its keys only if the query has equality conditions on all index keys that precede the sort keys. With index {a,b,c,d}, find({a:{$gt:2}}).sort({c:1}) does not use the index efficiently.
ESR guideline: put equality keys first, then sort keys, then range keys, so the index delivers sorted output without an in-memory sort. Sorting after equality also makes the sort non-blocking.

batchSize changes only how many documents each network round trip fetches. Driver iteration (next, hasNext, for-await) still yields one document at a time from the fetched batch. With batchSize 1 and 1000 results the driver issues 999 getMore calls.

Too large a batchSize makes the cursor allocate more resources than needed; too small adds network round trips. A batchSize of 0 opens the cursor and returns no documents in the first batch. Third-party sizing ranges (50-200 for large documents or memory limits, 500-2000 for small documents and bulk throughput) are heuristics, not vendor guidance.

MongoDB's documented range-query pagination: pick a field such as _id that changes consistently over time and has a unique index, filter with $lt (descending) or $gt (ascending), sort on it, and store the last-seen value for the next query. Range queries use indexes to avoid scanning unwanted documents.

For a non-unique sort field such as createdAt, keyset pagination needs a compound filter: $or of {createdAt < last} and {createdAt == last, _id < lastId}, sorted by {createdAt:-1,_id:-1}, backed by an index with the same fields and directions.

In the case that a single wildcard index could support multiple query fields, MongoDB can only use the wildcard index to support one of the query fields.

Instead, MongoDB uses the wildcard index to support only one of the query predicates. MongoDB automatically chooses which predicate to support based on relevant wildcard index paths. The unsupported query predicates are shown in the [`rejectedPlans`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/explain-results.md#mongodb-data-explain.queryPlanner.rejectedPlans) of the [explain results.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/explain-results.md#std-label-explain-results)
This is also true for compound wildcard indexes. The wildcard term of a compound index can only support one query predicate, although the non-wildcard terms can support the remaining predicates.

MongoDB mongos instances route queries and write operations to shards in a sharded cluster. mongos provides the only interface to a sharded cluster from the perspective of applications. Applications never connect or communicate directly with the shards.

The mongos tracks what data is on which shard by caching the metadata from the config servers. The mongos uses the metadata to route operations from applications and clients to the mongod instances. A mongos has no persistent state and consumes minimal system resources.

The most common practice is to run mongos instances on the same systems as your application servers, but you can maintain mongos instances on the shards or on other dedicated resources. See also Number of mongos and Distribution.
Establishing a cursor on all targeted shards.

The mongos then merges the data from each of the targeted shards and returns the result document. Certain query modifiers, such as sorting, are performed on each shard before mongos retrieves the results.
Aggregation operations running on multiple shards may route results back to the mongos to merge results if they don't need to run on the database's primary shard.
There are two cases in which a pipeline is ineligible to run on mongos.

Generally, the fastest queries in a sharded environment are those that mongos route to a single shard, using the shard key and the cluster meta data from the config server. These targeted operations use the shard key value to locate the shard or subset of shards that satisfy the query document.
mongos instances broadcast queries to all shards for the collection unless the mongos can determine which shard or subset of shards stores this data.
Multi-update operations are always broadcast operations.
The updateMany() and deleteMany() methods are broadcast operations, unless the query document specifies the shard key in full.

mongos can route queries that include the shard key or the prefix of a compound shard key a specific shard or set of shards. mongos uses the shard key value to locate the chunk whose range includes the shard key value and directs the query at the shard containing that chunk.
Depending on the distribution of data in the cluster and the selectivity of the query, mongos may still perform a broadcast operation to fulfill these queries.

The `{ metacritic : { $ne : null } }` query matches documents where the `metacritic` field exists **and** has a non-null value.

The `{ a: { $ne: null } }` query returns the complement, which is every document that `{ a: null }` does not match. The query matches the documents with `_id` values `2`, `3`, `5`, and `6`, including the document that holds an empty array.

The `{ "a.b": { $ne: null } }` query returns the complement, which is every document that `{ "a.b": null }` does not match: the documents with `_id` values `2`, `3`, `4`, and `5`. That result is not the same as the set of documents that have a non-null value for `a.b`. Neither `_id: 2` nor `_id: 3` has any value at `a.b`, yet the `{ $ne: null }` filter still matches them. A `{ $ne: null }` filter on a dotted path does not necessarily return the same documents as an [`$exists`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/exists.md#mongodb-query-op.-exists) check on that path.
